extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters and regulatory decisionmakers; environmental lawyers, public commenters, and environmental justice advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Crafting legal and technical comments evaluating EPA's section 112(f)(2) residual risk and 'ample margin of safety' analysis for Oil & Gas source categories, focusing on health-protective standards, cumulative impacts, control options, and environmental justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default HI limit for chronic non-cancer risks (≤0.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The default HI limit for chronic non-cancer risks should be well under 1.0 for individual sources—specifically, staff then recommended that it should be no higher than 0.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a 0.2 limit would allow an individual source to account for 20 percent of the contribution to total exposure in its vicinity and attempts to provide a de minimis fraction below which contributions are considered insignificant while not allowing a single source to dominate total exposures. EPA must reduce the TOSHI presumptive acceptability threshold to 0.2 or below to ensure protection of the most-exposed people in local communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of total exposure from multiple sources (cumulative exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must consider an individual’s total exposure to HAP in addition to exposure from the source category and facility when assessing non-cancer risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because RfCs assume thresholds for adverse effects, exposures from the facility in combination with emissions from all other sources may be sufficient to result in increased non-cancer risk; EPA has not evaluated other nearby HAP sources beyond the source category (except facility-wide) and must include cumulative impacts in its analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow a single source to 'consume' the non-cancer safety factor
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may not permit a single source covered by this rulemaking to consume the entire non-cancer risk safety factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a 0.2 contribution should not be assumed protective in communities with many prior exposures; where communities are exposed to many sources, EPA must assume that any risk above 0.1 is unacceptable. The acceptability determination must account for cumulative community exposures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use an arbitrary 50% cut-off for source significance
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's determination that a source 'drives' facility-wide risk based on whether it 'contributes 50 percent or more to the facility-wide maximum noncancer TOSHI of 1 or more' is arbitrary and unsupported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fifty percent is half the emissions; lower percentages can be significant contributions and may justify limits. EPA must justify any cutoff and cannot ignore high facility-wide risks based on an unexplained 50% threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set source-category limits when contribution is significant (tons and public health context)
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as the source category is contributing a significant amount to the facility-wide risk, EPA must set a limit for that source category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record shows these source categories contribute substantial HAP tons (e.g., 9,000 tons from Oil & Natural Gas Production); EPA must consider how much a source contributes and the public health impact of those emissions in the community context. Failure to provide actual amounts/percentages prevents informed comment and violates notice-and-comment requirements under section 307(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess socioeconomic disparity and environmental justice impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must evaluate and address disproportionate impacts of cancer, chronic, and acute risks on people of color and low-income populations, and incorporate that assessment into decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's demographic analysis shows disproportionate exposure; EPA cannot ignore this in its Executive Order 12898 statement. A level of risk that might otherwise be 'acceptable' becomes unacceptable when minority or lower-income people are disproportionately affected. EPA must use demographic data to reduce risk beyond the proposal where warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the baseline overall health status of affected communities
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must assess the starting point or baseline of 'overall health' status of affected individuals and communities using the best available local and national data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1999 Residual Risk Report supports considering population-level impacts and sensitive subpopulations (age, race, gender, income, pre-existing conditions, exposure history). This baseline assessment should inform risk determinations and protection measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on most-exposed individuals (within ~5 km analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must particularly analyze those who are the most exposed, within 5 km of oil and gas facilities, as part of its demographic and risk analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA did similar analysis in the chrome plating proposal; the residual risk evaluation should examine the most-exposed individuals to inform protective measures for sensitive subpopulations (children, low-income, minorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide plain-language statement of health risks and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must publish a plain-language statement of the health risks and benefits from its final action and in future rule proposals to make risks understandable to the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's MIR and numeric risk outputs are not easily understandable; the public needs descriptions of types of cancer, nature of disorders, target organs, and real-world impacts to provide meaningful comment. SAB recommends expanded discussion to understand real-world risks and health disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide an 'ample margin of safety to protect public health' per CAA §112(f)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the final step, EPA must set an appropriate residual risk standard that provides the requisite 'ample margin of safety to protect public health.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'ample' means more than adequate; EPA must adopt a more generous, health-protective approach than bare minimum. The ample margin determination should protect both cancer and non-cancer risks and may consider cost and technological feasibility in addition to public health factors, but health must be central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center ample margin analysis on public health, not cost alone
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must analyze whether proposed rules provide maximum feasible protection against risks to the greatest number of people, rather than relying primarily on cost-effectiveness to conclude adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's ample margin analysis currently lacks discussion on maximum feasible protection, how many people could be protected, or what margin is 'ample.' Cost can be considered, but the central inquiry is whether the proposed standards provide a plentiful margin of safety for public health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-cancer risks in 'ample margin' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must assess whether the proposed rule provides an 'ample margin of safety' to protect against non-cancer chronic and acute risks as well as cancer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has not discussed whether its rules provide an ample margin for non-cancer risks; the ample margin analysis is missing for non-cancer endpoints and must be conducted, including consideration of technologies' effects on non-cancer risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use health-based cost-effectiveness metrics (dollars per risk reduced)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should measure cost-effectiveness on a dollars per amount of cancer (or health) risk reduced basis rather than a ton-based metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For HAPs, small mass reductions can have large health benefits. Comparing cost to health protection (e.g., dollars per risk reduced) would allow assessment of whether additional cost is warranted to provide greater measurable protection and allow meaningful public comment on health-cost trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify and justify what constitutes an 'ample' margin (avoid superfluity)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must assess and explain the margin of safety achieved and why that margin is 'ample' rather than merely adequate or the bare minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to determine what additional emissions beyond the acceptable level are necessary to provide an ample margin would render the statutory term meaningless. EPA must identify what emission reductions would provide the ample margin and explain its reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on unrelated or unfinalized section 112(d) actions to satisfy 112(f)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cannot rely on proposed changes under section 112(d) when making its section 112(f)(2) ample margin determination; any measures relied upon must be proposed and analyzed under 112(f)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If EPA believes small glycol dehydrator limits proposed under 112(d)(2) provide an ample margin, it must propose and analyze them under 112(f)(2) so communities are assured of the protection regardless of whether 112(d) changes are finalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a reasoned explanation for claimed risk reductions from regulatory choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 112(f)(2), EPA must provide a reasoned explanation for how changes (e.g., removal of the benzene compliance alternative) achieve the cancer risk reductions it states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA asserted removal of a 0.9 Mg/year benzene option would reduce NGTS cancer risk from 90-in-1M to 20-in-1M, but supporting documentation is unclear or inconsistent. EPA must substantiate such claims in the record and cannot rely on unsupported memoranda or expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cumulative impacts, including background concentrations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's ample margin analysis must adequately and rationally account for cumulative impacts, including background concentrations and other nearby toxic emissions, as authorized by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 42 U.S.C. §7412(f)(1)(C) directs consideration of background concentrations; EPA's failure to assess exposures from other sources exaggerates the protective margin of the proposed rule. Facility-wide risk analyses must be supplemented by local cumulative exposure assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the full range of control options for ample margin
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must evaluate a broad array of control options and practices (technologies, processes, programs) that could achieve greater emission reductions when determining the ample margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should have considered desiccant dehydrators, Natural Gas Star program practices, BACT-level technologies, stronger LDAR, vendor literature innovations, state programs (CA, CO, WY), and other options referenced in technical reports. Limiting analysis to a few options is arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain searches and reasoned rejection of other control options
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must explain what other control options it searched for, what options it considered, and provide reasoned explanations for rejecting additional options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's analysis relied on only a limited set of options without explaining why others were excluded. A cursory or undocumented search and rejection is arbitrary and capricious; EPA must document its process and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support key modeling and assumption choices with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must support assumptions used in evaluating control options (e.g., assumptions about comparative cost-effectiveness of large vs small units) with data or reasoned explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: EPA assumed cost effectiveness for large glycol dehydrators would not exceed twice that of small units without providing a basis; typically larger units have better scaling economics. Unsupported assumptions must be substantiated or revised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use facility- and community-context in setting limits (protect most-exposed persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must ensure standards protect the most-exposed persons and consider facility-wide and community context when setting residual risk limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's preamble indicates protecting the greatest number of persons to 1-in-1M and protecting the most-exposed person to no more than 100-in-1M; EPA must demonstrate how proposed standards achieve these health-protection goals and evaluate additional feasible reductions to protect the most-exposed.
